title: Transitivity, Frobenius reciprocity and tensor identity for quotient induction
statement:
For an algebraically closed field $F$ of characteristic zero [def-weil-algebraic-closure], a representation of a finite group $J$ means a finite-dimensional [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] $F$-vector space $W$ with a homomorphism $J\to\operatorname{GL}_F(W)$. For $H\leq G$ put $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W=(F[G]\otimes_F W)/\langle [gh]\otimes w-[g]\otimes hw:g\in G,h\in H,w\in W\rangle_F$, with left $G$-action $a([g]\otimes w)=[ag]\otimes w$. Here $F[G]$ has basis $[g]$ and multiplication $[g][h]=[gh]$. Tensor products, quotient modules, finite direct sums and dimension have the meanings of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], [def-weil-pbc-quotient-module], [def-weil-pbc-direct-sum-modules] and [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. Write $\operatorname{Res}_H^G V$ for the same vector space with restricted action.
For all finite $G$, subgroups $K\leq H\leq G$, $H$-representations $W$, $K$-representations $U$ and $G$-representations $V$, induction preserves finite direct sums, has dimension $\dim_F\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W=[G:H]\dim_F W$, and has natural equivariant isomorphisms
$$\operatorname{Ind}_H^G(\operatorname{Ind}_K^H U)\simeq\operatorname{Ind}_K^G U,\qquad
V\otimes_F\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W\simeq\operatorname{Ind}_H^G(\operatorname{Res}_H^G V\otimes_F W).$$
There is a natural $F$-linear isomorphism
$$\operatorname{Hom}_G(\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W,V)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_H(W,\operatorname{Res}_H^G V),\qquad f\longmapsto(w\longmapsto f([1]\otimes w)).$$
For each finite $J$, let $R_F(J)$ be the abelian group presented as in [def-trf-abelian-group-presentation], generated by isomorphism classes with $[A\oplus B]=[A]+[B]$, and with multiplication $[A][B]=[A\otimes_F B]$. Restriction and induction therefore induce additive maps on these groups and obey $[V]\operatorname{Ind}_H^G x=\operatorname{Ind}_H^G(\operatorname{Res}_H^G[V]\,x)$ and $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\operatorname{Ind}_K^H=\operatorname{Ind}_K^G$.

proof.text: Write $[g,w]$ for the class of $[g]\otimes w$. It is linear in $w$, spans the quotient, and satisfies $[gh,w]=[g,hw]$. Indeed tensors span by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], and expanding the first factor in the specified group-algebra basis gives these generators. We will define linear maps on them by checking precisely this relation: the bilinear tensor map exists by that node; if the displayed relation maps to zero its span does too, and the map on cosets is independent of the representative by [def-weil-pbc-quotient-module]. Left multiplication by $a$ sends a relation to $[agh,w]-[ag,hw]$, so the stated $G$-action descends. The identities $1[g,w]=[g,w]$ and $a(b[g,w])=(ab)[g,w]$ prove the action laws.

proof.text: Choose a set $S$ of representatives of left cosets $G/H$. Each $g$ has a unique expression $g=sh$, $s\in S,h\in H$: existence is the coset definition, and cancellation gives uniqueness of $h$. Define $\alpha:\bigoplus_{s\in S}W\to\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W$ by $\alpha(\iota_s w)=[s,w]$, and define $\beta([sh,w])=\iota_s(hw)$. The latter is linear in $w$ and extends linearly in the group-algebra basis. For $h'\in H$ its two values on the balancing relation are $\iota_s(hh'w)$ and $\iota_s(h(h'w))$, equal by the action law; hence it descends as in Step 1. Now $\beta\alpha(\iota_s w)=\iota_s w$ and $\alpha\beta([sh,w])=[s,hw]=[sh,w]$. These spanning generators prove that $\alpha,\beta$ are inverse linear maps.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free], choose a basis $(b_i)_{i\in I}$ of $W$. It is finite: take a finite spanning family from [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], and let $I_0$ be the union of its finite basis supports. Every vector then has support in $I_0$, so each basis vector forces its index into $I_0$. In the coordinates of Step 2, the vectors $\iota_s b_i$ span by coordinatewise basis expansion, and a zero linear combination has all coefficients zero by inspecting each $s$ coordinate. Thus $[s,b_i]$ is a basis of induction. There are $|S||I|=[G:H]\dim_F W$ such vectors; [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] gives the stated dimension and finite-dimensionality, including $W=0$ (empty basis).

proof.text: For a finite family $(W_i)_{i\in I}$, the direct-sum comparison sends $[g,(w_i)]$ to $([g,w_i])_i$. Its inverse sends a family $(z_i)$ to $\sum_i\operatorname{Ind}(\iota_i)(z_i)$, where $\operatorname{Ind}(p)[g,w]=[g,pw]$ for an equivariant linear map $p$. This last formula respects the relation since $p(hw)=hp(w)$; it commutes with $G$ and respects identities and composition. The comparison respects relations coordinatewise. The composites are identities because $\sum_i\iota_i w_i=(w_i)$ and because projection after inclusion is the identity in the matching coordinate and zero otherwise. This also proves naturality. For $I=\varnothing$ both spaces are zero.

proof.text: For transitivity define $A([g,[h,u]])=[gh,u]$, with $g\in G,h\in H,u\in U$. The inner $K$-relation has images $[ghk,u]=[gh,ku]$. For the outer $H$-relation, the images of $[ga,[h,u]]$ and $[g,[ah,u]]$ are both $[gah,u]$. Linearity in $u$, then descent through the inner quotient and the outer tensor/quotient as in Step 1, therefore constructs $A:\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\operatorname{Ind}_K^H U\to\operatorname{Ind}_K^G U$.

proof.text: Define $C([g,u])=[g,[1,u]]$. For $k\in K$ the images of $[gk,u]$ and $[g,ku]$ coincide, since $[gk,[1,u]]=[g,[k,u]]=[g,[1,ku]]$. Thus $C$ descends. We have $AC([g,u])=[g,u]$ and $CA([g,[h,u]])=[gh,[1,u]]=[g,[h,u]]$, so $C=A^{-1}$. Left multiplication in $g$ commutes with both maps, proving $G$-equivariance. Applying any $K$-equivariant linear map to $u$ before or after $A$ gives the same $[gh,p(u)]$, proving naturality.

proof.text:
For the tensor identity define $\Phi(v\otimes[g,w])=[g,g^{-1}v\otimes w]$. This is linear in $v$ and $w$ and extends linearly in $[g]$. Its two values on the induction relation agree:
$$[gh,h^{-1}g^{-1}v\otimes w]=[g,g^{-1}v\otimes hw].$$
Here the first equality uses the target relation with the diagonal $H$-action on $\operatorname{Res}V\otimes W$. Thus for each $v$ it descends through the quotient; the resulting dependence on $v$ remains linear, and the tensor universal property gives $\Phi:V\otimes\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W\to\operatorname{Ind}_H^G(\operatorname{Res}V\otimes W)$.

source.place: Agent-written auxiliary representation calculation for inherited Step 3 duality route; tensor map and balancing check. Serre Part I Chapter 7 is WANTED, not present in this blueprint proof.

proof.text:
Conversely set $\Psi([g,v\otimes w])=gv\otimes[g,w]$. For each $g$ the rule is bilinear in $(v,w)$, so defines a linear map on $V\otimes W$. The target values of the source relation agree because
$$ghv\otimes[gh,w]=ghv\otimes[g,hw]=\Psi([g,hv\otimes hw]).$$
Pure tensors span, so this verifies the relation for every vector of $V\otimes W$; hence $\Psi$ descends. The composites on generators are $\Psi\Phi(v\otimes[g,w])=v\otimes[g,w]$ and $\Phi\Psi([g,v\otimes w])=[g,v\otimes w]$, proving they are inverse.

proof.text:
For $a\in G$,
$$\Phi(av\otimes[ag,w])=[ag,(ag)^{-1}av\otimes w]=[ag,g^{-1}v\otimes w]=a\Phi(v\otimes[g,w]).$$
Thus $\Phi$ and its inverse are equivariant. If $p:V\to V'$ is $G$-equivariant and $q:W\to W'$ is $H$-equivariant, applying the maps in either order sends $v\otimes[g,w]$ to $[g,g^{-1}p(v)\otimes q(w)]$, since $p(g^{-1}v)=g^{-1}p(v)$. This proves naturality in both variables.

source.place: Agent-written auxiliary representation calculation for inherited Step 3 duality route; equivariance and naturality of the tensor identity. Serre Part I Chapter 7 is WANTED, not present in this blueprint proof.

proof.text: For an equivariant linear $f:\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W\to V$, evaluation $E(f)(w)=f([1,w])$ is $H$-equivariant: $f([1,hw])=f([h,w])=h f([1,w])$. Conversely, for an $H$-equivariant linear $t:W\to\operatorname{Res}_H^G V$ define $L(t)([g,w])=g t(w)$. Its relation check is $gh t(w)=g t(hw)$, and its $G$-equivariance check is $ag t(w)=a(g t(w))$. Hence it is a well-defined equivariant linear map by Step 1.

proof.text: The composites are $E(L(t))(w)=t(w)$ and $L(E(f))([g,w])=g f([1,w])=f([g,w])$. Thus evaluation is bijective. Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication give $E(cf+df')=cE(f)+dE(f')$, so it is the required $F$-linear isomorphism. For equivariant $p:W'\to W$ and $q:V\to V'$, the value of $E(qf\operatorname{Ind}(p))$ at $w'$ is $qf([1,pw'])=q(E(f)(pw'))$, which is naturality in both variables.

proof.text: Finite-dimensional tensor products are representations: choose finite bases as in Step 3 and apply [lem-sc-tensor-product-free-basis]; the diagonal action obeys the group laws on pure tensors. The maps $(v\otimes(a,b))\mapsto(v\otimes a,v\otimes b)$ and the sum of the two inclusion maps are inverse equivariant maps by expansion on pure tensors. They prove tensor distributivity over direct sums; the corresponding maps in the other variable are identical with factors reversed. Tensor associativity, commutativity and the trivial one-dimensional unit are equivariant via $(u\otimes v)\otimes w\mapsto u\otimes(v\otimes w)$, $v\otimes w\mapsto w\otimes v$, and $c\otimes v\mapsto cv$, with the evident inverse formulas. All inverse checks are on spanning pure tensors. Hence multiplication respects the direct-sum relations in $R_F(J)$.

proof.text: Restriction preserves direct sums by its definition, and induction does so by Step 4. Both preserve isomorphisms: restriction keeps the inverse, and Step 4's induction formula sends inverse maps to inverse maps. They therefore induce additive maps on the presentations [def-trf-abelian-group-presentation], since each generating relation maps to zero. Finite-dimensional representations have a set of isomorphism classes: a finite basis identifies each with an action by matrices on some $F^n$. Step 12 makes multiplication biadditive. For a generating class $x=[W]$, Step 7 gives $[V]\operatorname{Ind}x=\operatorname{Ind}(\operatorname{Res}[V]x)$; for $x=[U]$, Step 5 gives transitivity. Every class is a finite integer linear combination of generators, so additivity extends both equalities to all classes, including negative coefficients.
